question: Copyright infringement in the digital age is a serious problem that needs to be tackled urgently. The European Union Intellectual Property Office points to a decline in television, film, music, software and publication piracy until 2021. In 2022, however, the trend was reversed, when piracy rose by 3.3 %.

The increase should be a wake-up call for the bodies responsible for curbing piracy, a practice that not only breaches copyright and intellectual property rights but also robs countries of tax revenue and leads to cybercrime. In Portugal, the audiovisual sector estimates that EUR 200 million in revenue is lost every year. Newspaper sharing in private groups also has a considerable impact on the media sector. 1.
What results can be seen of the Commission recommendation on combating online piracy of live events?
Is the Commission considering tougher measures, for instance standardising the crime of copyright theft throughout the EU in order to include the breach of rights in the digital ecosystem?
Does the Commission intend to introduce legislation to discourage piracy by sending warnings and applying administrative sanctions?
answer: The Commission takes combatting online piracy seriously. Directive 2004/48/EC (1) and Directive 2001/29/EC (2) provide legal remedies for rightsholders if their exclusive rights are infringed.

In addition, the Digital Services Act (3) sets out a horizontal framework applicable to online intermediaries to ensure their accountability and to counter the spread of illegal content, including content infringing intellectual property rights.
In May 2023, the Commission adopted the recommendation on combating online piracy of sports and other live event s (4) to address unauthorised retransmissions of live events.

The Commission and the European Observatory on Infringements of Intellectual Property Rights in the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) work closely to monitor the implementation of the recommendation and its effects on online piracy of sports and other live events. No results are available at this stage. In July 2023, Key Performance Indicators (5) (KPIs) were published to guide data collections.

The EUIPO Observatory will collect pertinent data for 2024 in January 2025 and for the first half of 2025 in July 2025. By 17 November 2025, the Commission will assess the impact of the recommendation taking into account the results from the monitoring exercise.
This assessment will inform whether there is a need for additional measures at EU level, including to prevent the illegal dissemination of other types of copyright protected content.

In March 2024, in its Recommendation on measures to combat counterfeiting and enhance the enforcement of intellectual property rights (6) the Commission encouraged Member States to reassess if the criminal penalties available in national laws for commercial scale piracy are sufficient to provide a deterrent and duly correspond to the harm caused.
